hook: The giant of French writing, author of Les Misérables, who spent 19 years in exile.

pages.x: Victor Hugo was born in 1802 in Besançon, the son of one of Napoleon's generals, and grew up between Paris, Italy and Spain. At 14 he wrote in a notebook: "I want to be Chateaubriand or nothing", naming the most famous writer of the day.

In 1830 his play Hernani broke all the old rules of French drama. On opening night young Romantics fought the traditionalists in the theatre, and the battle went on night after night. Hugo became the leader of the Romantic movement.
His wife later wrote that, to make himself finish his next novel on time, he locked away his clothes so he could not go out, and wrote wrapped in a big grey woollen shawl.

That novel, of 1831, tells of Quasimodo, the deaf bell ringer of Notre-Dame, and his love for Esmeralda. Hugo wrote it partly to save the neglected cathedral, and it worked: Paris began to restore it.
In 1843 his beloved daughter Léopoldine drowned in the Seine with her husband, six months after her wedding. Hugo learned of it from a newspaper. For years he wrote poems to her.

When Louis-Napoleon seized power in 1851, Hugo called him "Napoleon the Little" and had to flee. He spent 19 years in exile, most of them on the island of Guernsey, writing at a standing desk that looked out to sea.

In 1862 he published Les Misérables, the story of Jean Valjean, a convict who stole a loaf of bread, hunted for years by the policeman Javert. It is a huge novel about poverty, justice and mercy, and today a famous musical.
A famous story says that, wanting to know how Les Misérables was selling, he sent his publisher a note with just "?". The publisher wrote back: "!"
He came home when the emperor fell in 1870. When he died in 1885, his coffin lay in state under the Arc de Triomphe, and some two million people followed it to the Panthéon.
Hugo is France's best loved writer, and fought all his life against the death penalty, poverty and tyranny.
pts: Fought the death penalty and tyranny
